messages.author: 2710b717e5dbb066
messages.subject: Help understanding Prior Choice Recommendations
parts:
This is my first time posting to this group (though I have been reading it for a few months).

I have been reading the "Prior Choice Recommendations" document on the stan-dev site and some of the articles mentioned there. to try and better understand Bayesian modeling.  I find that I understand things best when I actually try something out, so I have simulated some data to analyze and have tried a few different Stan programs to analyze the data and wanted to get some comments on the advantages and disadvantages of each approach.

Part of this is motivated by the idea that choosing a meaningful and informative prior takes care of the multiple comparison problem.

To motivate my simulations I thought of studying Systolic Blood Pressure (SBP) in people with high blood pressure.  So for a single group I would use a normal prior with mean 150 and standard deviation 50, 140 is considered high blood pressure (by some definitions), so the mean of a group would need to be higher than that, hence the 150.  And if someone has a blood pressure below 50 or over 250 then they would be in the hospital at best, so a standard deviation of 50 means 95% between those 2 values.  

What I have read so far mainly refers to regression type models where the prior on a coefficient would be centered at 0, but I was thinking more along the lines of analysis of variance, comparing 3 groups (1 control and 2 different treatments).  So my first approach is to just fit a mean to each group, all having the same prior, but otherwise independent to see if having the same prior would pull the means close enough to each other to overcome possible multiple comparison problems.  My Stan code for this is:

data {
  int<lower=0> n1;
  int<lower=0> n2;
  int<lower=0> n3;
  vector[n1] x1;
  vector[n2] x2;
  vector[n3] x3;
}
parameters {
  real mu1;
  real mu2;
  real mu3;
  real<lower=0> sigma;
}
model {
  mu1 ~ normal(150, 50);
  mu2 ~ normal(150, 50);
  mu3 ~ normal(150, 50);
  sigma ~ cauchy(0, 20);
  
  x1 ~ normal(mu1, sigma);
  x2 ~ normal(mu2, sigma);
  x3 ~ normal(mu3, sigma);
}
generated quantities {
  real d12;
  real d13;
  real d23;
    
  d12 = mu1 - mu2;
  d13 = mu1 - mu3;
  d23 = mu2 - mu3;
}


This is what I would call the naive approach, it seems pretty straight forward, fit 3 means and a common standard deviation, then look at the credible intervals for the differences between the means.  

When I simulated data and fit this model, the coverage of the d12 credible interval was actually slightly lower than what it should have been.  So this approach was not correct for even a single difference, let alone adjusting for multiple comparisons.  

My next thought was to have the prior on the means come from a multivariate normal with non-zero correlations.  This might work, but it seems more complicated than needed to fit, and the correlation or covariance on prior means does not seem like a natural parameter to think about.  So I skipped this approach (but would consider looking at it again if anyone can argue in favor of it).

My second approach is to convert the aov to a regression type model where I now fit a mean for group 1, but then have parameters representing the difference between group 2 and group 1 and the difference between group 2 and group 1.  The Stan code is:

data {
  int<lower=0> n1;
  int<lower=0> n2;
  int<lower=0> n3;
  vector[n1] x1;
  vector[n2] x2;
  vector[n3] x3;
}
parameters {
  real mu1;
  real d12;
  real d13;
  real<lower=0> sigma;
}
model {
  mu1 ~ normal(150, 50);
  d12 ~ normal(0, 10);
  d13 ~ normal(0, 10);
  sigma ~ cauchy(0, 20);
  
  x1 ~ normal(mu1, sigma);
  x2 ~ normal(mu1+d12, sigma);
  x3 ~ normal(mu1+d13, sigma);
}
generated quantities {
  real d23;
  
  d23 = d13 - d12;
}

This time the d12 CI in simulations had greater than 95% coverage indicating that the more informative priors on the differences did have a beneficial effect (I have not looked at the family wise error rate yet).  So this seems much more in line with the claim of not needing to adjust for multiple comparisons.  But this also depends somewhat on the parameterization, I have only included indirect prior information on d23 here.  Also the effective sample size is lower for this model than the initial one, this makes sense since any update to mu1 will affect the means in the other 2 groups as well.  But more iterations can fix that.

My third model was to use a hierarchical model, since that had been suggested as well:

data {
  int<lower=0> n1;
  int<lower=0> n2;
  int<lower=0> n3;
  vector[n1] x1;
  vector[n2] x2;
  vector[n3] x3;
}
parameters {
  real mu1;
  real mu2;
  real mu3;
  real<lower=0> sigma;
  real mu;
  real<lower=0> sig2;
}
model {
  mu ~ normal(150, 50);
  sig2 ~ cauchy(0,10);
  mu1 ~ normal(mu, sig2);
  mu2 ~ normal(mu, sig2);
  mu3 ~ normal(mu, sig2);
  sigma ~ cauchy(0, 20);
  
  x1 ~ normal(mu1, sigma);
  x2 ~ normal(mu2, sigma);
  x3 ~ normal(mu3, sigma);
}
generated quantities {
  real d12;
  real d13;
  real d23;
  
  d12 = mu1 - mu2;
  d13 = mu1 - mu3;
  d23 = mu2 - mu3;
}

This also had good coverage of the d12 CI, but had the smallest effective sample size (for the same total iterations) and some of the Rhat values were 1.01 (the 1st 2 models had them all at 1).  Again this is probably just a matter of increasing total iterations.

The thing I like about this model is that I am back to thinking about 3 means rather than reparameterizing to differences with the amount of the relationship being handled in the hyper parameters.  But there are a couple of things about this model that bother me a little.  First I am treating what I would think of as fixed effects more like random effects (maybe that is still too frequentist thinking that I just need to get over) and second, I am fitting an extra level of complexity that I am not directly interested in.

I would appreciate any comments on when and/or why to use model 2 vs. model 3 (or even variations on model 1 if appropriate).  Also, how would any of these models use the idea of "scaling the parameters to unity"?

Thanks,

messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Help understanding Prior Choice Recommendations
parts:
Hey, just three quick recommendations:
1.  Supply your prior parameters ("150", "50", etc.) as data rather than hard-coding them into the model.
2.  Vectorize mu and the prior means and sd's.  (I'd also recommend making x into a ragged array, but Stan doesn't have ragged arrays yet.)
3.  Make your parameters scale free.  For example, for SPB, make a new scale where 0 is a baseline and most values are between -1 and +1, then all priors will be on unit scale as we recommend in that document.
A
